result: Budding yeast topo II (ScTop2) forms higher-order spherical assemblies (puncta) at physiological protein concentrations (>250 nM), with puncta size and number increasing with protein concentration.
evaluation: Claims C2, C38-C40, and C45 are supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2C showing concentration-dependent puncta formation. The observations are consistent across multiple protein concentrations and the physiological relevance is established by comparison to reported cellular concentrations.

result: DNA stimulates condensation of ScTop2 and is integrated into the puncta. DNA exhibits a biphasic effect: low concentrations (5-10 nM) increase puncta size and number, while higher concentrations (>50 nM) cause resolubilization. Plasmid DNA forms elongated fibrillar structures at intermediate concentrations, while short DNAs remain spherical.
evaluation: Claims C3, C42-C44, C46, and C52-C55 are supported by dual-channel confocal microscopy (Figure 2D-E, Figure 3A) showing DNA colocalization and biphasic concentration dependence. The morphological differences between plasmid and short DNA substrates are documented in Figure 2E.

result: Condensate formation by ScTop2 requires extended DNA segments (≥100 bp) and is not stimulated by polyanionic substrates like heparin, indicating specificity for DNA rather than general polyanion binding.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by DNA length titration experiments (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) showing that 50 bp DNA does not enhance condensation while 100 bp, 200 bp, and plasmid DNA do. The heparin control (C49) demonstrates specificity for DNA.

result: ScTop2 puncta exhibit liquid-like properties in the presence of DNA. Without DNA, puncta are gel-like (no FRAP recovery), but with 5 nM DNA, approximately one-third of protein recovers within 15 minutes. Puncta also undergo fusion events on the order of minutes.
evaluation: Claims C57-C61 are supported by FRAP experiments (Figure 3B) showing DNA-dependent fluidity and time-lapse microscopy (Figure 3C) demonstrating fusion events. The distinction between gel-like (no DNA) and liquid-like (with DNA) behavior is clearly documented.

result: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of ScTop2 is necessary for LLPS. Deletion of the CTD (ScTop2ΔCTD) prevents condensate formation even at high protein concentrations (1 μM) and in the presence of DNA.
evaluation: Claims C5, C62, and C66 are supported by confocal microscopy data (Figure 4A) showing that ScTop2ΔCTD does not form condensates under conditions where full-length protein does. This establishes the CTD as necessary for LLPS.

result: The isolated ScTop2 CTD cannot form condensates alone but does so in the presence of DNA (at 50 mM KOAc) or crowding agents like PEG. DNA acts as a scaffold to promote CTD co-localization, though DNA integration is less homogeneous than with full-length protein.
evaluation: Claims C63-C65, C67, and C123 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing CTD condensation requires DNA or PEG. The partial DNA integration (C64) is documented in Figure 4A.

result: ScTop2 condensation is primarily driven by ionic protein-DNA interactions. Salt titration shows that DNA-free puncta dissolve at 200 mM KOAc, while DNA-containing condensates persist until 400 mM KOAc. Intermediate salt concentrations still support DNA-mediated resolubilization.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 and C77 are supported by salt titration experiments (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing differential salt sensitivity. The conclusion about ionic interactions (C77) is further supported by the amino acid composition data (Figure 2B) and 1,6-hexanediol experiments.

result: 1,6-hexanediol promotes aggregation of ScTop2 into large irregular bodies and prevents DNA-mediated resolubilization, but has little effect on the isolated CTD. High concentrations (10%) disrupt ScTop2 enzymatic activity.
evaluation: Claims C71, C72, and C76 are supported by confocal microscopy and activity assays (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The differential effect on full-length vs. CTD suggests the catalytic core is affected by 1,6-HD.

result: Phosphorylation status of ScTop2 does not control LLPS ability but modulates condensate physical properties. Phosphatase-treated ScTop2 forms more numerous small puncta at low DNA concentrations and more fibrillar bodies at intermediate DNA concentrations. Critically, dephosphorylation eliminates DNA-induced fluidity in FRAP experiments.
evaluation: Claims C80-C86 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), mass spectrometry (Figure 4D), and FRAP data (Figure 4E-F). The mass spec confirms complete dephosphorylation of CTD residues, and FRAP shows loss of DNA-induced mobility.

result: Condensation induces ScTop2 to switch from DNA unlinking to active DNA catenation. At 150 mM KOAc and 100 nM ScTop2 (no condensates), ~80% supercoil relaxation occurs. At higher protein concentrations where condensates form, DNA converts to well-shifted catenated products. At 400 mM KOAc (no condensates), only relaxed topoisomers are observed. The catenated products can be decatenated by dissolving condensates with high salt.
evaluation: Claims C4, C88-C93, and C140 are supported by combined confocal microscopy and activity assays (Figure 5A-B) showing correlation between condensate formation and catenation. The restriction enzyme experiments (Figure 5B) confirm the well-shifted species are catenanes that can be decatenated by salt-induced condensate dissolution.

result: Deletion of the ScTop2 CTD shifts enzymatic activity from catenation to robust DNA knotting. ScTop2ΔCTD shows nearly complete supercoil relaxation at 100 nM, but at higher concentrations (250-1000 nM) produces extensive DNA knotting as evidenced by ladder patterns on gels after nicking. The catalytic core is highly efficient at forming DNA knots at physiological enzyme concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C6, C94-C98, C100, and C142 are supported by activity assays with nicking experiments (Figure 5C-D) showing characteristic knot ladder patterns. The interpretation is supported by citations to prior work on DNA knotting and comparison to Figure 1.

result: Full-length ScTop2 also forms knots, but catenanes are the principal product when condensation occurs. The CTD routes knotting activity into robust catenane production.
evaluation: Claims C99 and C101 are supported by nicking experiments with full-length ScTop2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) showing that while knots are present, catenanes predominate under condensate-forming conditions. This contrasts with the CTD-deleted enzyme.

result: Human TOP2α and TOP2β can form condensates with DNA. TOP2α weakly forms bodies alone at 1 μM but shows marked increase with 50 nM DNA. TOP2β produces larger puncta alone and is only moderately enhanced by DNA. DNA colocalizes with both proteins.
evaluation: Claims C103-C108 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 6A) showing differential condensation behavior between the two human isoforms and DNA colocalization in both cases.

result: TOP2α and TOP2β have different condensate-forming potentials. TOP2α shows limited puncta formation alone (≤3 μm² at 1 μM) but strong DNA-dependent enhancement. TOP2β forms larger bodies at lower concentrations (50-100 nM) that exceed DNA-free ScTop2 size. Both show biphasic DNA response with stimulation at low-moderate concentrations and resolubilization at high concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C109-C114 are supported by systematic concentration titrations (Figure 6B-C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing quantitative differences in condensation behavior between isoforms while maintaining qualitative similarity in DNA response.

result: The ability to couple catenation to condensation is conserved across eukaryotic topo IIs. TOP2α shows supercoil relaxation at 100 nM but switches to catenation at ≥250 nM when puncta appear. TOP2β shows similar behavior at slightly lower concentrations (250 nM), consistent with enhanced condensation properties.
evaluation: Claims C115-C119 and C141 are supported by combined confocal microscopy and activity assays (Figure 6D-E) showing correlation between condensate formation and catenation for both human isoforms, paralleling the ScTop2 results.

result: The CTDs of eukaryotic topo IIs are long intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) with characteristic amino acid composition: high lysine (≥15%), moderate serine (~10%), aspartate and glutamate (10%), and very low aromatic content (<5%). Despite varied isoelectric points (pI 5.5-9.6), their composition is more similar to eukaryotic replication initiators than to typical low-complexity LLPS proteins like FUS or DDX4.
evaluation: Claims C31, C35-C37 are supported by disorder prediction analysis (Figure 2A) and amino acid composition analysis (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The comparative analysis with other LLPS proteins is documented.

result: Puncta formation by ScTop2 is time-dependent, appearing within 10 minutes and plateauing in number and size after ~60 minutes.
evaluation: Claim C41 is supported by time-lapse microscopy data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) showing kinetics of puncta formation.

result: The isolated CTD requires lower salt (50 mM KOAc) to form condensates with DNA, showing robust CTD-DNA interactions evidenced by large puncta and DNA colocalization. Higher salt concentrations make puncta more diffuse.
evaluation: Claims C73-C75 and C124 are supported by salt titration experiments with isolated CTD (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing salt-dependent condensation behavior.

result: Full-length ScTop2 forms condensed bodies in the absence of DNA at physiological salt (150 mM KOAc) and protein concentrations (0.5-1.5 μM). These DNA-free assemblies are gel-like (no FRAP recovery) but dissolve at ≥200 mM KOAc, demonstrating they are not irreversible aggregates.
evaluation: Claims C126-C128 are supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 2C), FRAP data (Figure 3B), and salt titration (Figure 4B). The physiological relevance is established by citation to cellular concentrations.

result: The difference in salt and DNA sensitivities between isolated CTD and full-length enzyme is likely due to additional DNA contacts through the cleavage core (20-30 bp binding) and ATPase region. Since ≥100 bp DNA is needed for LLPS, DNA likely acts as a bridge. Multiple protein-DNA contacts and CTD-CTD interactions facilitate phase separation.
evaluation: Claims C130-C133 are supported by the DNA length requirement data (Figure 2E) and are consistent with structural knowledge of topo II DNA binding (supported by citations). The inference about bridging is reasonable given the data.

result: ScTop2 and TOP2α show closely matched LLPS response with strong DNA dependency, while TOP2β more readily forms condensates alone and is less influenced by DNA at higher concentrations. This difference may be attributable to isoelectric points: basic for ScTop2 and TOP2α, acidic for TOP2β.
evaluation: Claims C172-C174 are supported by comparative confocal microscopy data and amino acid composition analysis (Figure 2B, Figure 6). The correlation with pI is a reasonable inference from the data.

result: A mechanistic model for knotting: The sharp DNA bend introduced by the cleavage core contributes to knot formation. At low protein concentrations, enzymes preferentially resolve pre-existing crossovers (e.g., supercoils). As protein concentration increases, more DNA bends lead to compaction and increased likelihood of crossovers forming between segments of the same plasmid, which when acted upon by topo II generate knots. The density of knot crossovers should be proportional to plasmid compaction, which depends on local topo II:DNA ratio.
evaluation: Claims C146-C151 present a mechanistic model supported by the knotting data (Figure 5D), structural knowledge (citations to Dong and Berger, 2007; Vologodskii et al., 2001), and comparison to prior work (Hsieh, 1983; Wasserman and Cozzarelli, 1991). The model is consistent with the experimental observations.

result: A mechanistic model for catenation: The CTD creates bridges between plasmid molecules that locally concentrate DNA and topo II, facilitating crossover formation between different DNA molecules leading to catenanes. CTD-less ScTop2 forms some catenanes at intermediate concentrations (250-500 nM) but only knots at 1000 nM. As protein concentration increases, strand passage in cis (knots) outcompetes passage in trans (catenanes) unless the CTD is present to favor inter-DNA links. At intermediate concentrations, mixtures of products reflect equilibrium between local enzyme/DNA concentration and access to cis vs. trans crossovers.
evaluation: Claims C152-C158 present a mechanistic model supported by the comparative activity data for full-length vs. CTD-deleted enzyme (Figure 5C-D, Figure 7C-D). The model explains the observed product distributions and is consistent with the LLPS data.

result: Both knotting and catenation, but not supercoil relaxation, are abolished by high salt (400 mM). Elevated ionic strength prevents CTD-facilitated LLPS and weakens DNA-catalytic core interactions, antagonizing loop formation and shifting activity toward resolving pre-existing crossovers.
evaluation: Claim C159 is supported by activity assays at different salt concentrations (Figure 4B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) showing selective abolition of knotting and catenation while relaxation persists.

result: Background knowledge and discussion claims about topo II mechanism, prior work on LLPS, prior work on DNA topology, prior work on topo II localization and function, and speculative implications for cellular function.
evaluation: These claims (C1, C7-C30, C32-C34, C51, C56, C78-C79, C87, C102, C120-C122, C125, C129, C134-C139, C143-C145, C160-C188) are primarily background knowledge supported by appropriate citations or are discussion/speculation based on the experimental findings. They provide context and interpretation but are not primary experimental results.
